children.title: CHAPTER 8 Transformers
children.path: Speech and Language Processing, Chapter 8: Transformers.pdf/Root/CHAPTER 8 Transformers
children.summary: This page introduces Chapter 8, titled 'Transformers,' from the textbook 'Speech and Language Processing' by Daniel Jurafsky and James H. Martin. The text outlines the chapter's focus on using transformer architectures for causal language modeling. It features Figure 8.1, a diagram illustrating a transformer decoder for processing a single input token through layers including embedding, multihead attention, feedforward networks, and unembedding to produce output probabilities.

children.title: 8.1 Attention
children.path: Speech and Language Processing, Chapter 8: Transformers.pdf/Root/8.1 Attention
children.summary: This section introduces the concept of attention in transformer models, contrasting it with static embeddings like word2vec where a word's representation is fixed regardless of context. It explains that attention allows for dynamic representations by integrating information from surrounding tokens. The text uses examples to illustrate how pronouns (e.g., 'it') and ambiguous words (e.g., 'bank') are disambiguated based on their context within a sentence. Figure 8.2 illustrates the architecture of a left-to-right transformer, showing how input tokens are encoded, passed through stacked transformer blocks, and processed by a language modeling head to predict the next token.

children.title: 8.1.1 Attention more formally
children.path: Speech and Language Processing, Chapter 8: Transformers.pdf/Root/8.1 Attention/8.1.1 Attention more formally
children.summary: This page from Chapter 8 on Transformers explains the concept of self-attention, which allows models to weigh and combine information from different tokens in a sequence. It features Figure 8.3, a schematic diagram illustrating how the model attends to specific words ('chicken' and 'road') when computing the representation for the word 'it'. The text describes this mechanism as a way to build richer contextualized representations layer by layer.

children.title: Simplified version of attention
children.path: Speech and Language Processing, Chapter 8: Transformers.pdf/Root/8.1 Attention/8.1.1 Attention more formally/Simplified version of attention
children.summary: This page, from section 8.1 on Attention, explains the mechanics of causal self-attention in language models. It features Figure 8.4, which illustrates how a model processes input tokens by attending to all prior inputs up to the current position. The text further details a simplified version of attention where output vectors are computed as weighted sums of prior token representations based on similarity scores derived via dot products and softmax normalization.

children.title: A single attention head using query, key, and value matrices
children.path: Speech and Language Processing, Chapter 8: Transformers.pdf/Root/8.1 Attention/8.1.1 Attention more formally/A single attention head using query, key, and value matrices
children.summary: This page from Chapter 8 on Transformers details the mechanics of a single attention head. It defines the roles of query, key, and value vectors in the attention process and introduces the weight matrices (W^Q, W^K, W^V) used to project input vectors into these representations. The text provides a set of equations (8.9 through 8.14) for computing self-attention, including the scaled dot-product calculation and the final output vector computation.

children.title: Multi-head Attention
children.path: Speech and Language Processing, Chapter 8: Transformers.pdf/Root/8.1 Attention/Multi-head Attention
children.summary: This page, from section 8.1 on Attention, details the mechanics of self-attention in transformer models. It features Figure 8.5, a diagram illustrating the step-by-step calculation of the output for the third element (a3) of a sequence using causal self-attention. The text explains the dimensionality of vectors and matrices involved, such as query, key, and value vectors, and references the original Transformer paper by Vaswani et al. (2017). The page concludes by introducing the concept of Multi-head Attention.

children.title: 8.2 Transformer Blocks
children.path: Speech and Language Processing, Chapter 8: Transformers.pdf/Root/8.2 Transformer Blocks
children.summary: Section 8.2 introduces the architecture of a transformer block, which is built around self-attention and includes feedforward layers, residual connections, and layer normalization. It explains the concept of the 'residual stream' where information flows through the block, with components reading from and adding to this stream. The section also describes the 'prenorm' version of the architecture, where layer normalization occurs before the attention and feedforward layers.

children.title: Feedforward layer
children.path: Speech and Language Processing, Chapter 8: Transformers.pdf/Root/8.2 Transformer Blocks/Feedforward layer
children.summary: The section describes the feedforward layer as a fully-connected 2-layer network with one hidden layer and two weight matrices. It explains that weights are shared across token positions but differ between layers, and notes that the hidden dimensionality (d_ff) is typically larger than the model dimensionality (d). The section provides the mathematical formula for the Feedforward Network (FFN) using ReLU activation.

children.title: Layer Norm
children.path: Speech and Language Processing, Chapter 8: Transformers.pdf/Root/8.2 Transformer Blocks/Layer Norm
children.summary: The section explains Layer Norm (layer normalization), a technique used to improve training performance in deep neural networks by normalizing the values of a hidden layer. It describes the process as a variation of z-score applied to a single vector within a transformer block, rather than an entire layer. The text details the calculation steps: computing the mean (μ) and standard deviation (σ) over the vector's elements, normalizing the vector components by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation, and finally introducing two learnable parameters, γ (gain) and β (offset), for the final output.

children.title: Putting it all together
children.path: Speech and Language Processing, Chapter 8: Transformers.pdf/Root/8.2 Transformer Blocks/Putting it all together
children.summary: The section titled 'Putting it all together' synthesizes the previously discussed components of a transformer block into a single, comprehensive set of equations (8.26-8.31). It defines the step-by-step computation within one transformer block, detailing the sequence of operations including layer normalization, multi-head attention, residual connections, and the feedforward network (FFN). The text also explains how these blocks are stacked to form larger models, referencing specific examples like T5, GPT-3-small, and GPT-3 large.

children.title: 8.3 Parallelizing computation using a single matrix X
children.path: Speech and Language Processing, Chapter 8: Transformers.pdf/Root/8.3 Parallelizing computation using a single matrix X

children.title: Parallelizing attention
children.path: Speech and Language Processing, Chapter 8: Transformers.pdf/Root/8.3 Parallelizing computation using a single matrix X/Parallelizing attention
children.summary: This page from Chapter 8 on Transformers explains how to parallelize computation within a transformer block by packing input embeddings into a single matrix X. It details the process of computing query, key, and value matrices (Q, K, V) via matrix multiplication with weight matrices, and visualizes the resulting N x N QK^T similarity matrix in Figure 8.9. The text concludes by presenting the final equations for calculating the attention output.

children.title: Masking out the future
children.path: Speech and Language Processing, Chapter 8: Transformers.pdf/Root/8.3 Parallelizing computation using a single matrix X/Masking out the future
children.summary: This page, titled 'Parallelizing Computation Using a Single Matrix X', explains the concept of masking future tokens in self-attention mechanisms to prevent models from seeing information they shouldn't. It details how an upper-triangular mask matrix is applied to the QK^T product to zero out scores for future positions. The page includes Figure 8.10, illustrating the masked QK^T matrix, and Figure 8.11, which provides a comprehensive schematic of the parallelized attention computation steps, including the generation of Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V) matrices.

children.title: Parallelizing multi-head attention
children.path: Speech and Language Processing, Chapter 8: Transformers.pdf/Root/8.3 Parallelizing computation using a single matrix X/Parallelizing multi-head attention
children.summary: The section explains the mechanics of parallelizing multi-head attention. It details how input and output dimensions relate to model dimension $d$, key/query dimension $d_k$, and value dimension $d_v$. It describes the weight layers ($W^Q_c, W^K_c, W^V_c$) used to produce Query, Key, and Value matrices for each head, which are then processed through self-attention. The outputs of all heads are concatenated and projected via a final linear projection $W^O$ to yield the self-attention output.

children.title: Putting it all together with the parallel input matrix X
children.path: Speech and Language Processing, Chapter 8: Transformers.pdf/Root/8.3 Parallelizing computation using a single matrix X/Putting it all together with the parallel input matrix X
children.summary: This section details the mathematical formulation of a transformer layer when processing a parallel input matrix X. It presents equations (8.38 and 8.39) for computing the output O and H, which involve MultiHeadAttention and Feed-Forward Networks (FFN) applied to LayerNorm inputs. The text further breaks down the internal computation of a single transformer block into five sequential steps (equations 8.40–8.45), defining intermediate tensors T1 through T5 to represent operations like LayerNorm, attention, residual connections, and FFN.

children.title: 8.4 The input: embeddings for token and position
children.path: Speech and Language Processing, Chapter 8: Transformers.pdf/Root/8.4 The input: embeddings for token and position
children.summary: This section explains how the input to a transformer model is constructed using token and positional embeddings. It details that each token is represented by an embedding vector from an embedding matrix E, which can be selected via indexing or one-hot vector multiplication (Figure 8.12). Since these token embeddings are not position-dependent, they are combined with positional embeddings to create a composite input X. The text describes two methods for generating positional embeddings: absolute position embeddings, which are learned parameters stored in a matrix E_pos (Figure 8.14), and sinusoidal embeddings using sine and cosine functions.

children.title: 8.5 The Language Modeling Head
children.path: Speech and Language Processing, Chapter 8: Transformers.pdf/Root/8.5 The Language Modeling Head
children.summary: This page, titled 'The Language Modeling Head', explains the final component of a transformer architecture used for language modeling. It details how the model predicts the next word in a sequence by taking the output from the last token and projecting it into a probability distribution over the vocabulary. The text describes the linear layer that produces logit scores and introduces the concept of weight tying, where the projection matrix is tied to the transpose of the input embedding matrix (often called the unembedding layer).

children.title: 8.6 More on Sampling
children.path: Speech and Language Processing, Chapter 8: Transformers.pdf/Root/8.6 More on Sampling
children.summary: This page from Chapter 8 on Transformers details the architecture of a language model head, illustrated in Figure 8.15. It explains how logits are converted into word probabilities via a softmax layer and discusses text generation methods like greedy decoding. The text also clarifies terminology regarding 'decoder-only models' versus encoder-decoder architectures and introduces Section 8.6, which covers sampling techniques for balancing quality and diversity.

children.title: 8.6.1 Top-k sampling
children.path: Speech and Language Processing, Chapter 8: Transformers.pdf/Root/8.6 More on Sampling/8.6.1 Top-k sampling
children.summary: This page, from section 8.6 'More on Sampling', illustrates the architecture of a decoder-only transformer language model in Figure 8.16, showing how an input token is processed through multiple layers to predict the next token. The text below introduces 'Top-k sampling' as a method for generating text that is more creative and diverse than greedy decoding by selecting from the top k most probable words rather than just the single most likely one.

children.title: 8.6.2 Nucleus or top-p sampling
children.path: Speech and Language Processing, Chapter 8: Transformers.pdf/Root/8.6 More on Sampling/8.6.2 Nucleus or top-p sampling
children.summary: This section discusses Nucleus or top-p sampling as an alternative to fixed k top-k sampling. It explains that while top-k sampling uses a fixed number of words, the probability distribution shape varies by context. Top-p sampling (or nucleus sampling) instead keeps the top p percent of the probability mass, dynamically adjusting the pool of word candidates based on probability rather than count. The section includes a formula defining the top-p vocabulary V^(p) as the smallest set of words such that the sum of their probabilities is greater than or equal to p.

children.title: 8.7 Training
children.path: Speech and Language Processing, Chapter 8: Transformers.pdf/Root/8.7 Training
children.summary: Section 8.7 Training describes the training process for large language models, which involves using cross-entropy loss (negative log likelihood) to adjust network weights via gradient descent. It explains that transformers allow parallel processing of training items and details how large models are trained by filling a full context window with text, packing shorter documents together, and utilizing very large batch sizes.

children.title: 8.8 Dealing with Scale
children.path: Speech and Language Processing, Chapter 8: Transformers.pdf/Root/8.8 Dealing with Scale

children.title: 8.8.1 Scaling laws
children.path: Speech and Language Processing, Chapter 8: Transformers.pdf/Root/8.8 Dealing with Scale/8.8.1 Scaling laws
children.summary: This page, titled 'Dealing with Scale' (Section 8.8), discusses the characteristics of large language models (LLMs) and the concept of scaling laws. It features Figure 8.17, which illustrates the architecture of a transformer model used for language modeling, showing input tokens, stacked transformer blocks, and the calculation of loss. The text provides specific details about the Llama 3.1 405B Instruct model from Meta as an example of a massive scale model. Section 8.8.1 introduces scaling laws, explaining that model performance is determined by model size, dataset size, and compute budget, citing Kaplan et al. (2020).

children.title: 8.8.2 KV Cache
children.path: Speech and Language Processing, Chapter 8: Transformers.pdf/Root/8.8 Dealing with Scale/8.8.2 KV Cache
children.summary: This page from Chapter 8 on Transformers discusses scaling laws for model parameters, providing equations to compute the number of parameters (N) and applying them to GPT-3. It then introduces the concept of KV Cache in section 8.8.2, explaining how it optimizes inference by storing key and value vectors to avoid recomputation.

children.title: 8.8.3 Parameter Efficient Fine Tuning
children.path: Speech and Language Processing, Chapter 8: Transformers.pdf/Root/8.8 Dealing with Scale/8.8.3 Parameter Efficient Fine Tuning
children.summary: This page, from section 8.8.3 titled 'Parameter Efficient Fine Tuning', discusses methods for fine-tuning large language models without updating all parameters. It introduces PEFT (Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning) and details the LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) technique, which freezes original model weights and updates a low-rank approximation instead. The text includes Figure 8.18 illustrating parts of attention computation that can be cached.

children.title: 8.9 Interpreting the Transformer
children.path: Speech and Language Processing, Chapter 8: Transformers.pdf/Root/8.9 Interpreting the Transformer

children.title: 8.9.1 In-Context Learning and Induction Heads
children.path: Speech and Language Processing, Chapter 8: Transformers.pdf/Root/8.9 Interpreting the Transformer/8.9.1 In-Context Learning and Induction Heads
children.summary: This page from Chapter 8 on Transformers features Figure 8.19, which illustrates the intuition behind LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) by showing how pretrained weights are frozen while fine-tuning occurs via a pair of matrices A and B. The text introduces Section 8.9, 'Interpreting the Transformer,' focusing on mechanistic interpretability. It then details Section 8.9.1 regarding In-Context Learning and Induction Heads, explaining that in-context learning was first proposed by Brown et al. (2020) in their introduction of GPT3.

children.title: 8.9.2 Logit Lens
children.path: Speech and Language Processing, Chapter 8: Transformers.pdf/Root/8.9 Interpreting the Transformer/8.9.2 Logit Lens
children.summary: This page from a technical book discusses the 'induction head' mechanism in transformers, explaining how it predicts repeated sequences through prefix matching and copying. It includes Figure 8.20, which illustrates this process using an example sentence about owning vintage cars. The text also covers ablation studies by Olsson et al. (2022) and Crosbie and Shutova (2022) that demonstrate the causal role of induction heads in in-context learning. Finally, section 8.9.2 introduces the 'logit lens' as a tool for visualizing internal transformer representations.

children.title: 8.10 Summary
children.path: Speech and Language Processing, Chapter 8: Transformers.pdf/Root/8.10 Summary
children.summary: This section summarizes the key concepts of the transformer architecture introduced in Chapter 8. It covers transformers as non-recurrent networks based on multi-head self-attention, the structure of a transformer block (residual stream, layer normalizations, attention and feedforward layers), input computation via embeddings and positional encoding, the language model head for generating logits, the wide context window capability, and computational tricks like KV cache and parameter-efficient finetuning.

children.title: Historical Notes
children.path: Speech and Language Processing, Chapter 8: Transformers.pdf/Root/Historical Notes
children.summary: The 'Historical Notes' section outlines the origins of the transformer architecture, citing Vaswani et al. (2017) and explaining that it was developed from two prior research lines: self-attention and memory networks. It details how encoder-decoder attention was introduced by Graves (2013) and Bahdanau et al. (2015), and how this concept was extended to self-attention by researchers like Ling et al., Cheng et al., and Liu et al. The text also attributes the terminology of key, query, and value to memory networks, referencing works by Sukhbaatar et al., Weston et al., and Graves et al.
